summary: AERO-AGRI is a free, bilingual (English/Vietnamese) web tool that helps farmers, extension officers and researchers in Vietnam choose whole-year crop rotations that need less fresh water, keep the soil covered and avoid the salt-water season. It combines six NASA datasets (2015–2025) with FAO-56 water-balance methods at two pilot sites. In Bến Tre (Mekong Delta), replacing the Winter–Spring rice crop with soybean cuts supplemental fresh water by about 41% (15,329 to 8,978 m³/ha a year), and the ranking holds in every crop year from 2015/16 to 2024/25. In Đắk Lắk (Central Highlands), the tool shows the coffee trade-off: a cover crop needs about 19% more dry-season water but cuts soil loss by about 87% (plot-study factors, not yet verified locally). Local knowledge goes in instead of assumptions: farmers mark the months their canal water turns salty and enter how they irrigate, and the answer follows their own field. A "lessons from the past 10 years" panel turns past seasons into planning figures for next year. Independent NASA satellite data (MODIS, GPM IMERG, SMAP) check the model, and every number shows its source.
details:
The problem

In Bến Tre (Mekong Delta), salt water moves up the canals from about February to April, exactly when farmers need fresh water; two rice crops a year need about 15,329 m³ of supplemental fresh water per hectare, and the land lies bare through the dry season. In Đắk Lắk (Central Highlands), Robusta coffee is irrigated from groundwater from January to April; extension services recommend cover crops against erosion, but a living cover also uses water. Farmers need to compare options for their own field, not for an average one.

 

What AERO-AGRI does

One page, four steps:

1. Your field: enter the crop and sowing date of each season, the months your canal water turns salty (Bến Tre), or how you irrigate (Đắk Lắk), and a hotter or drier year to test.

2. Compare options: fresh water needed per year and in the salty months, bare-soil months, a typical year and a dry year (1 in 5), each year since 2015, and "lessons from the past 10 years".

3. Satellite checks: independent NASA data tested against the model.

4. Plan and report: a printable report for the extension officer and a season-by-season CSV.

Farmers read water per 1,000 m²; advisers test scenarios; scientists see every formula, source and limit. A guided demo mode walks a new user through the main path.

 

How it works

Daily NASA POWER weather (2015–2025) drives the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration. Crop water need is ETc = Kc × ETo with FAO-56 coefficients. Effective rainfall follows FAO Training Manual 3 for rice and USDA-SCS for upland crops and coffee, and flooded rice adds land-preparation and percolation water. Deficits are summed month by month, so the tool can report the fresh water each option needs in any month a farmer marks as salty. MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI shows the observed crop calendar next to the modeled one.

 

What we found (modeled from NASA data)

- Bến Tre: replacing Winter–Spring rice with soybean cuts fresh water from 15,329 to 8,978 m³/ha a year (41% less); maize gives 9,025 m³/ha. The ranking holds in all 10 crop years, including the 2016 drought, and in a scenario 1.5 °C warmer with 20% less rain (still about 39% less).

- If salt water arrives early (December to April), two rice crops need about 5,831 m³/ha of fresh water in those months; soybean needs about 1,939 m³/ha.

- Đắk Lắk: a cover crop needs about 19% more water in January–April but cuts soil loss by about 87% (RUSLE C-factors from a plot study in Indonesia; not yet verified locally).

- Rice–shrimp is shown separately: its shrimp phase uses brackish water and is not modeled, and the tool lists the soil sodicity risk from a field study.

 

Local knowledge and past years

We changed the tool after feedback from the Hanoi judges. Instead of assuming salty months and irrigation practice, it asks for them. Salty months start from the National Agricultural Extension Center's published estimate, and farmers can correct them from their own canal or the provincial salinity bulletin. Coffee growers enter litres per tree, rounds and trees per hectare; the tool shows their seasonal volume and how much drier or wetter each past season was (for example, the 2024 dry season needed 28% more than average, about one extra round at the grower's own rate). It does not tell experienced growers how much to irrigate. The "lessons from the past 10 years" panel shows how often each option needed less water, the driest year, the dry-year volume to secure for next year, the latest season, and any past year as an analogue. None of this is a weather forecast.

 

How we checked it

- MODIS MOD09A1 flooding signals detected Winter–Spring rice sowing about 16 days after the date assumed in the model (6 seasons); for 2023 the satellite date (17 Nov) is 5 days from the date reported in the local press (about 22 Nov).

- GPM IMERG and NASA POWER annual rainfall agree within 1.2% (r = 0.90 month by month in Bến Tre, 0.89 in Đắk Lắk).

- SMAP root-zone soil moisture tracks the modeled coffee water deficit over 10 dry seasons (r = −0.94).

- 82 automated tests check the calculations.

 

Tools and technologies

Python, pandas and NumPy; a Python HTTP server with REST endpoints; HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Chart.js); Google Earth Engine to extract MOD09A1, IMERG, SMAP and SRTM; pytest. The public demo on GitHub Pages runs the same Python code in the browser with Pyodide, and the bundled NASA data let the app run offline with "python run.py".

 

Limits and next steps

The NASA POWER grid cell is about 50 km; the soil type at the Ba Tri pilot site is not yet verified (the tool also shows a low-percolation bound); soil water storage, daily salinity, the shrimp phase, yields, costs and prices are not modeled. Next: field soil and salinity measurements in Ba Tri, a model of the shrimp phase, and trials with extension officers in more Mekong provinces.

 

Use of AI (SI)

Google Antigravity (Gemini) and Claude Code assisted with coding, code review, data analysis, translation, interface design and the slides. The team chose the problem, sites, strategies and research plan, and checked the results. All numbers come from NASA data processed by the project code or from cited sources; no AI-generated data, images or report text are used.
